figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: Drex pointer architecture (DLM, v1.5, and v2.0, not including Drex Max, which is shown in Figure 2). The state and the questions (left) are tokenized into one sequence that consists of a state segment $S$ followed by one question block $b_{k}$ for each question. Each question block is a contiguous block of text that contains the instruction, the options, and a final <decide> token, in this order; each option is enclosed between an opening tag <opt> and a closing tag </opt>. The backbone $f_{\theta}$ encodes the sequence under the block-causal pattern shown inside it (Eq. 17): every token of a question block can attend to all tokens of the state and to the preceding tokens of the same question block, but not to any token of another question block. The pointer head turns the hidden state at <decide> into a query $\mathbf{q}$ and each </opt> state into a key $\mathbf{k}_{j}$, and returns a softmax over exactly the supplied options (right). The example outputs are consistent with Eq. 1: (0.62−1/3)/(1−1/3)=0.43 and $\hat{s}=0.83+2\times 0.12=1.07$.
figures.headline: The pointer head turns the decide state into a query and each option-end state into a key, giving a softmax over supplied options only.
citing_sentences: Every Drex pointer model is a pretrained language-model backbone $f_{\theta}$ plus a pointer head $(W_{q},W_{k})$ (Figure 1).

figures.label: Figure 2
figures.caption: Two ways to score the options of a question. Each small square is one token, colored by its type as in Figure 1; the legend at the bottom lists the token types. (a) The pointer models (DLM, v1.5, and v2.0) encode one sequence per request: the state $S$, followed by one question block per question. Each question block attends to the state but not to other question blocks, so the state is encoded once and shared by all questions. The pointer head scores each option as the scaled dot product of the hidden state at the option’s </opt> token (the key) and the hidden state at the <decide> token of its question block (the query). (b) Drex Max encodes each question as its own sequence: the image tokens that an image encoder (ViT) produces from the input images, the state $S$, the instruction, the options, and a final answer marker, the single token <ans>. Each option is written after its option code (A, B, …), which is a single token, and a colon. The 48 Gated DeltaNet layers of the backbone process the sequence from left to right, and its 16 full-attention layers (every fourth layer) attend in both directions. A readout head, i.e., a bias-free linear layer, maps the final hidden state at <ans> to one logit per option code (255 in total), and a softmax over the logits of the $K$ supplied options gives their probabilities. The pointer models trade accuracy for a shared, cacheable state; Drex Max trades the cache for full bidirectional context in every question.
figures.headline: Pointer models share one encoded state across questions, while Drex Max encodes each question as its own sequence, with non-causal full-attention layers.

figures.label: Figure 3
figures.caption: Post-training pipeline of the pointer models (shown for Drex v1.5). Stage 1 fine-tunes every weight in the backbone and a randomly initialized pointer head by optimizing the supervised objective of Eq. 9. Stage 2 (RLAF) replaces one-hot labels with an adjusted target $\tilde{q}$, which is constructed from a teacher distribution and the verified outcome. RLAF then maximizes the expected reward $R$ of Eq. 10, which is largest when the predicted distribution equals $\tilde{q}$. Drex Max is trained with full-parameter SFT (with the same consistency losses), then the low-rank variant of RLAF as described in Section 6.5, then SFT of the image encoder (Appendix D).
figures.headline: Pointer model training runs supervised fine-tuning, then RLAF against adjusted targets built from a teacher and the verified outcome.
citing_sentences: The pointer models use the RLAF formulation of Section 6.3 (Figure 3); Drex v2.0 additionally includes a task-specific specialization stage between supervised fine-tuning and RLAF to improve its performance on a particular family of tasks (Section F.1).

figures.label: Figure 4
figures.caption: Training data of Drex v1.5: 1,150,460 verified text decision records over eleven domains. Each bar shows the number of records in the respective domain.
figures.headline: Drex v1.5 training data totals 1,150,460 verified text records, with counts shown per domain across eleven domains.
citing_sentences: We assembled the training data of Drex v1.5, consisting of a mix of exactly 1,150,460 textual decision records across eleven domains (Figure 4; exact counts in Table 13).

figures.label: Figure 5
figures.caption: Per-domain skill on Decision Index 0.4.1 (public subset, scores from the leaderboard, except for GPT-6 Luna Decisions, which we evaluated locally). Drex Max leads in every domain except Arts, where Drex v2.0 is 0.5 points higher, and Knowledge, where it ties with Jev 1.14.0 at 57.1.
figures.headline: Drex Max leads each Decision Index domain except Arts, where v2.0 is 0.5 points higher, and ties Jev 1.14.0 in Knowledge.
citing_sentences: On the public subset, Drex Max scores 67.52 vs. 61.25 for v2.0, 58.08 for v1.5, 60.70 for Jev 1.14.0, and 47.78 for GPT-6 Luna Decisions (Table 1, Figure 5).

figures.label: Figure 6
figures.caption: Other decision benchmarks. One dot per model; Drex models are colored purple, and axes do not start at zero. The dashed line indicates the Jev 1.14 reference win rate of 50% in the game arena, and it indicates the “shorter transcript $\Rightarrow$ success” heuristic (AUROC 0.709) on OSWorld-Verified. The game-arena win rates (bottom-left panel) come from a separate evaluation that was run when Drex Max was launched (Table 17 in the Appendix) and have no confidence intervals. The results in the other three panels come from our own evaluations.
figures.headline: Drex Max has the lowest expected calibration error on DecideBench, at 1.1%, and the highest win rate among decision models in the launch game arena.
citing_sentences: It reaches the lowest ECE on DecideBench (1.1%), has the highest win rate among decision models in the launch game arena, and is the only model that clearly outperforms a transcript-length heuristic when judging finished OSWorld episodes, with the lowest Brier score (Figure 6; Sections H.3 and H.6).

figures.label: Figure 7
figures.caption: Calibration of the deployed models on the evaluation subset of Decision Index 0.4.1. (a) Calibration curves: the accuracy of the decisions in each bin (of predicted probabilities) versus the average predicted probability of the decisions that bin, showing only bins with at least 30 decisions; a perfectly calibrated model lies on the diagonal. (b) Precision@top-$k$%: the accuracy on the $k$% of decisions on which the model is most confident, for $k=25,50,75,100$. (c) Expected calibration error (ECE) in each Decision Index domain for the three Drex models, at the deployed temperature (bars) and at the temperature $T^{\star}$ fitted on a subset of Decision Index (circles). GPT-6 Luna Decisions is not shown in (c) because we do not have its per-domain breakdown.
figures.headline: Keeping the most confident 80% of Drex Max decisions raises precision from 87.9% to 96.1%, and the top 50% reaches 99.3%.
citing_sentences: Fitting the temperature on a subset of Decision Index gives $T^{\star}=0.91$; because $T^{\star}<1$, dividing the logits by $T^{\star}$ results in sharpened output distributions (i.e., more peaked), which raises the confidence of the model and reduces its ECE on the evaluation subset to 0.79% (Table 4, Figure 7a).

Keeping only the 80% of decisions on which Drex Max is most confident raises its precision from 87.9% (precision@top-100%, i.e., accuracy on all decisions) to 96.1% (precision@top-80%), and keeping the most confident 50% raises it further to 99.3% (precision@top-50%; Figure 7b).

figures.label: Figure 8
figures.caption: Option order. (a) The flip rate under a random permutation of the options, that is, the fraction of decisions whose top option changes, for decisions with $K{=}2$, $3\leq K\leq 5$, and $K\geq 6$ options. (b) The accuracy of each model under the original, reversed, and permuted orderings of the options, and the accuracy of the ensemble of the three orderings, which averages the three probability distributions that the model returns for a decision, option by option, and takes the option with the highest average probability (Table 5). Under the reversed and permuted orderings and the ensemble, the accuracy of every model differs from its accuracy under the original ordering by at most 1.2 percentage points.
figures.headline: Random permutations change the top option in 4.3% of Drex Max decisions, compared with 5.9% for v2.0, 5.3% for v1.5 and 4.3% for Jev.
citing_sentences: We find that random permutations of the option set change the most probable option in 4.3% of Drex Max’s decisions, 5.9% of v2.0’s, 5.3% of v1.5’s, and 4.3% of Jev’s (Table 5, Figure 8).

figures.label: Figure 9
figures.caption: Drex v2.0 across training stages. Stage 1 (S1) is supervised fine-tuning, Stage 2 (S2) is the specialization stage (Section 6.4), and Stage 3 (S3) is reinforcement learning from adjusted feedback (RLAF). Most of the improvement in the Decision Index 0.2.1 skill score occurs in Stage 1. Stage 2 mainly improves the skill in the Retrieval domain and the accuracy on JevBench-231, and Stage 3 gives small further gains in the skill in the Tools and Arts domains. In the game arena against Jev 1.13.0 (Table 6), the 95% confidence intervals of the score overlap at every checkpoint.
figures.headline: Most of Drex v2.0's Decision Index gain arrives in supervised fine-tuning, with later stages adding smaller gains in specific domains.
citing_sentences: We evaluated seven checkpoints that were saved during the training of Drex v2.0 (Tables 6 and 9).

figures.label: Figure 10
figures.caption: Attention masks for a request with a four-token state, a three-way choice question ($b_{1}$), and a noul question ($b_{2}$). Filled cells mark the query–key pairs that are allowed to attend, and lighter cells mark tokens in the question block that attend to the shared state. (a) Block-causal mask of Eq. 17. (b) Drex DLM adds bidirectional attention within the state. (c) Optional option isolation, in which <decide> still attends to every option. Hybrid backbones implement (a) by processing each question as a separate causal sequence $[S;b_{k}]$ that starts from the cached state. The masks are generated by the code that implements them in the released models.
figures.headline: Question blocks attend to the shared state but never to each other under the block-causal mask, which option isolation further restricts.
citing_sentences: On attention-only backbones, the sequence is encoded under a block-causal mask (Figure 10, Appendix Eq. 17): every token of a question block can attend to all tokens of the state and to the preceding tokens of the same question block, but not to any token of another question block.
This mask is shown in Figure 10a.

Efficient-DLM is trained with bidirectional attention inside blocks [19], so Drex DLM enables the state_bidir option, which additionally sets $M_{ij}=1$ whenever both tokens belong to the state, i.e., $\operatorname{seg}(i)=\operatorname{seg}(j)=0$ (Figure 10b).

figures.label: Figure 11
figures.caption: Per-benchmark change from Drex v2.0 to Drex Max on Decision Index 0.4.1 (chance-corrected skill, our evaluations), grouped by domain and sorted within each domain. Max scores higher on 28 of the 37 benchmarks, and its only two large drops are on POP909-CL and Habermas Machine.
figures.headline: Max scores higher than v2.0 on 28 of 37 benchmarks, with its only two large drops on POP909-CL and Habermas Machine.
citing_sentences: The largest per-benchmark gains in our experiments are on GSM8K ($66.8{\to}83.2$ accuracy; 10), BBH ($78.3{\to}93.7$; 68), ACOS ($23.9{\to}39.8$ F1; 9), WinoGrande ($86.1{\to}94.8$; 63), MuSR ($59.6{\to}70.3$; 66), and the home-appliance simulator ($54.5{\to}70.5$) (Figure 11 in the Appendix, Appendix J).
Its only two large drops are on POP909-CL and Habermas Machine (Figure 11; discussed in Section 8.1).
Differences between the rows of Table 1 and the per-benchmark changes in Figure 11 should therefore not be attributed to any single factor.

figures.label: Figure 12
figures.caption: Decision Bench v4 by category, sorted by Drex Max accuracy (images in image encoder); category sizes in parentheses. The frontier models’ advantage is concentrated in Product management and AI agents & evals, and Drex Max’s largest deficit is Trust & safety.
figures.headline: Frontier models' advantage over Drex Max is concentrated in Product management and AI agents & evals, and its largest deficit is Trust & safety.
citing_sentences: By category (see Figure 12 in the Appendix, Appendix K), Max is weakest on Product management, Documents & meetings, and AI agents & evals.
Figure 12 shows the accuracy by category, and Appendix K gives per-category and per-task tables.

figures.label: Figure 13
figures.caption: Inference latency of Drex v1.5. (a) Median latency of the previous and the current version of our inference code. A new question about a cached state of 114–117k tokens is answered faster than an uncached state of 2k tokens can be processed. (b) For an uncached state at the maximum length of 131,072 tokens, almost all of the time is spent in the state pass, which processes the state once per request, and the total exceeds our target of 2 s.
figures.headline: A new question on a cached 114–117k-token state takes 21.6 ms, faster than an uncached 2k-token state at 35.6 ms.
citing_sentences: For Drex v1.5, a new question about a cached state of 114–117k tokens is answered in 21.6 ms, which is faster than processing an uncached state of 2k tokens (35.6 ms; Figure 13a).

Processing an uncached state remains the main cost: it takes 1.78 s for a state of 114–117k tokens and about 2.7 s at the maximum length of 131,072 tokens, almost all of it in the state pass (Figure 13b).

abstract: Autoregressive approaches with large language models such as long chain-of-thought reasoning have become the default for new AI applications because they reach higher accuracy on a wide range of tasks. In production, however, such approaches give inconsistent answers, require parsing of outputs, and add cost and latency. This has driven a resurgence of discriminative inference in the form of decision models, which, given a question and a set of options supplied by the user, return a probability distribution over the options without autoregressive decoding. Decision models match frontier LLMs on well-defined tasks at a fraction of the cost. We present Drex, a family of four open decision models; the largest, Drex Max, is competitive with frontier models on real-data decisions while remaining fast, calibrated, and stable under reordering of the options. Each request consists of a state (a document, record, or agent context, optionally with images) and questions related to that state, with each asking for a choice among a set of options, a yes/no judgment, or a score on an ordered scale. The four models have 8B (DLM), 9B (v1.5), 35B with 3B active (v2.0), and 27B (Max) parameters. Training combines supervised fine-tuning with reinforcement learning from adjusted feedback (RLAF), plus vision tuning for Max. Controlled ablations show that RLAF improves accuracy and consistency. On Decision Index 0.4.1, Max sets a new state-of-the-art among the decision models we compare (67.52 on the public suite vs 60.70 for Jev 1.14.0). On the independently run Artificial Analysis Decision Index, it has the second-highest score among decision models (64 vs. 65 for the three leading models). On Decision Bench v4, it beats Jev 1.14 and our other models, is statistically tied with d3-turbo and GPT-6 Sol, and trails Claude Opus 5.5 by 1.6 points; it has the highest accuracy among decision models on DecideBench and is competitive with the top model on JevBench-231. Max answers a typical request in 183 ms, against about 2.0 s for GPT-6 Sol and 3.5 s for Claude Opus 5.5, and demonstrates output stability under option reordering. All four models are open source; the weights and inference code are collected at github.com/nace-ai/drex-decision-models.

sections.body: The section motivates decision models for settings where the option set changes per request, which fixed classification heads and autoregressive decoding handle poorly. It defines the interface and four research questions on calibration, option order, training, and capacity with modality. The pointer models (DLM, v1.5, v2.0) encode the context once and share it across questions. Drex Max re-encodes the context for each question and reads answers from a readout head over option codes. The authors state that most evidence is comparative, so only one ablation of Drex Max training supports causal claims.
sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.headline: Decision models read answers as option probabilities without decoding, for option sets supplied at inference time.

sections.body: This section places decision models among option-scoring methods, cross-encoders and pointer networks, option-order sensitivity studies, and calibration work with proper scoring rules. The four Drex models use different backbones: a diffusion language model, a Gated DeltaNet hybrid, and a sparse mixture-of-experts model (Qwen3.6-35B-A3B). The interface follows the System One API of Jev, and the pointer models are built on the open Kev code base. Drex Max adopts the attention pattern and readout design of pplx-decider, but the authors trained its weights themselves from Qwen3.8-27B.
sections.heading: 2 Related work
sections.headline: The Drex models sit between option scoring, pointer networks, and calibration work, and each uses a different backbone.

sections.body: The section defines a decision request as a state plus typed questions: choice, noul (yes/no), and score (an integer scale, returning an expected level). Each question has up to 255 options and a probability distribution over them. Five desirable properties are listed: closed-world output, question independence, invariance to option order, calibration, and grounding in every supplied modality. The architectures guarantee the first two by construction, while the other three are learned and measured. Evaluation uses expected calibration error over 15 bins, log loss, Brier score, selective accuracy, and top-1 flip rate.
sections.heading: 3 Problem formulation
sections.headline: A decision request holds a state and typed questions, and the model returns a distribution over each question's supplied options.

sections.body: Every pointer model is a pretrained backbone plus a pointer head with query and key projections, `W_q` and `W_k`. Requests are packed into one token sequence with a state segment and one block per question, separated by special delimiter tokens that user text cannot produce. On attention-only backbones a block-causal mask applies; hybrid backbones process each question as a separate causal sequence starting from the cached state. The projection dimension is 256 on every released checkpoint, giving 2.1M head parameters for v1.5 and 1.0M for v2.0, under 0.03% of either backbone. Inference needs one encoding of the state and a short pass per question, with no autoregressive decoding.
sections.heading: 4 Pointer architecture
sections.headline: Pointer models encode the context once and score each option with a dot product between query and option-end states, with no decoding.

sections.body: Drex Max uses Qwen3.8-27B, a dense model with 64 layers: 48 Gated DeltaNet layers and 16 full-attention layers. The causal mask is removed only in the full-attention layers, so those layers attend in both directions. A bias-free linear readout head maps the final hidden state to 255 logits, one per option code, and a softmax over the supplied options gives probabilities; the temperature is 1.009, fitted on held-out records. The head has about 1.3M parameters. Because the state is re-encoded for each question, the median latency is 183 ms, against 151 ms for v2.0 and 145 ms for v1.5. The authors note that the trained weights do not reproduce intended scores under the original causal mask.
sections.heading: 5 Drex Max: a dense multimodal decision model
sections.headline: Drex Max removes the causal mask in full-attention layers of a 27B backbone and reads answers from a readout head over option codes.

sections.body: The v1.5 training mix contains exactly 1,150,460 textual decision records across eleven domains, mostly distilled from stronger teachers, with the rest from open-source datasets and procedurally generated data. Every label is checked against a gold answer, an execution result, or a game engine, and Decision Index and JevBench evaluation items are excluded. Supervised fine-tuning adds permutation and state-shuffle consistency losses. The RLAF stage builds adjusted targets from a teacher distribution and the verified outcome, and optimizes a proper-scoring reward. Drex Max uses a KL-regularized variant, and Drex v2.0 adds a specialization stage with low-rank adapters, which the released v1.5 and Max do not use.
sections.heading: 6 Training
sections.headline: Training combines supervised fine-tuning with consistency losses and reinforcement learning from adjusted feedback, with vision tuning for Max.

sections.body: Decision Index 0.4.1 scores are chance-corrected skills, where 0 is uniform guessing and 100 is perfect, and raw scores are reported separately; unanswered or unsupported requests count as wrong. The public subset holds 140,620 requests, of which 140,178 were not discarded by the maintainers. Decision Bench v4 has 1,071 single-question decisions: 949 text-only, 62 text and image, and 60 image. Baselines include Jev 1.13.0 and 1.14.0, GPT-6 Luna Decisions, d3-turbo, GPT-6 Sol, and Claude Opus 5.5, with chat models prompted for JSON probabilities. Accuracy intervals are Wilson, and differences use percentile bootstrap over 5,000 resamples. The authors do not adjust p-values for multiple comparisons.
sections.heading: 7 Experimental setup
sections.headline: Models are compared on Decision Index 0.4.1, Decision Bench v4 and other suites, using Wilson intervals and exact McNemar tests on paired questions.

sections.body: This section reports Decision Index results (8.1), Decision Bench v4 (8.2), calibration (8.4), option-order stability (8.5), multimodal decisions (8.6), training stages (8.7), and controlled Drex Max comparisons (8.8). On the public Decision Index subset, Max scores 67.52, against 60.70 for Jev 1.14.0 and 61.25 for v2.0. On Decision Bench v4, the Max image-encoder variant reaches 94.0% accuracy with a Wilson interval of [92.4, 95.3]. Most comparisons are paired and reported with intervals, and the text states where differences are not significant.
sections.heading: 8 Results
sections.headline: Results cover accuracy, calibration, option order, images and training stages, compared against decision-specialized and frontier chat models.

sections.body: Decision models run one prefill pass per request, and the state pass dominates cost. A question on a cached 114k–117k-token context is answered in 21.6 ms, faster than an uncached 2k-token state at 35.6 ms, while a fresh 131,072-token state takes about 2.7 s, above the 2 s target. Shared prefill gives speedups of 6–8× at 8k tokens and 11–12× at 32k tokens with 16 questions, with bit-identical outputs, but it is not applied below 1,024 tokens. Graph capture cut single-question latency at 1k tokens by about two thirds. Answer-changing optimizations are checked against a per-model accuracy threshold; graph padding with small-batch FP8 moved accuracy by −0.34 points.
sections.heading: 9 Deployment and inference optimization
sections.headline: Shared prefill, graph capture and kernel changes cut latency, and answer-changing optimizations are accepted only within an accuracy threshold.

sections.body: The pointer and readout heads differ in attention, backbone size, and training data at once, so the authors say the source of Max's gains is untested. Every Drex model trails frontier chat models on closed-book knowledge, with the largest gap on HLE and GPQA; the Knowledge skill rises from 44.6 for v1.5 to 47.9 for v2.0 and 57.1 for Max. Max is over-confident: outside Language, its mean confidence exceeds accuracy by 5–9 percentage points, and its ECE is 8.4% on questions with 6 to 20 options. On six or more options, 13% of its decisions change top option under random permutation. The authors suggest routing low-confidence decisions to human review.
sections.heading: 10 Discussion and limitations
sections.headline: Stated limits: gaps to frontier chat models on closed-book knowledge, over-confidence in Max, and untested causes of its gains.

sections.body: Drex outputs a probability distribution over options the user supplies, and the paper answers its four research questions. On calibration, the deployed-temperature ECE is 1.4–4.5% on Decision Index decisions and falls to 0.8–1.4% after tuning on those examples. For option order, random permutation changes the top option in 4.3–5.9% of decisions and accuracy by at most 1.2 percentage points. For training, RLAF adds 2.0 points to the Decision Index score for Max, and the consistency terms lower the flip rate from 6.3% to 4.2%. Max reaches 94.0% on Decision Bench v4, 1.6 percentage points below Claude Opus 5.5, and open questions remain on closed-book knowledge.
sections.heading: 11 Conclusion
sections.headline: Drex Max leads the public Decision Index at 67.52, and its gains over the pointer models are not isolated to one design choice.

sections.body: The appendix gives an extended related-work discussion, the question types and metric definitions (Table 10), packing and attention masks for the pointer models, and the scoring formulas used for the Decision Index. It also reports inference efficiency for Drex Max, including a kernel change that reduced latency by 9–16% for states of 8k to 128k tokens and changed accuracy by −0.13 points. Deployment configurations for each model are listed in a table. The Decision Index skill formula is written out, and failed or unsupported requests are counted as wrong.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix covers related work, question types and metrics, pointer masks, Drex Max kernel timings, deployment setups and Decision Index scoring.
